event.canonical_title: Brother of NYPD Officer Who Died from 9/11-Related Cancer Advocates for Victims
event.summary: As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, Phil Alvarez, a retired NYPD detective, reflects on his brother Luis's death from cancer linked to toxins at Ground Zero. Alvarez is working to extend the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund to assist others affected by similar health issues. This year, a seventh moment of silence will be observed to honor those who have died from illnesses related to the toxic dust from the attacks.

event_overview.title: About 9/11 Victim Compensation
event_overview.subject: 9/11 Victim Compensation
event_overview.summary: The September 11th Victim Compensation Fund (VCF) is a U.S. federal compensation program for people physically harmed by the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks or subsequent debris-removal work, and for personal representatives of people who died from those causes. Reopened under the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act and later permanently authorized, it addresses eligible 9/11-related health claims rather than serving as a general memorial or emergency-relief program.

facts.label: Origins and purpose
facts.value: Congress created the original September 11th Victim Compensation Fund in Title IV of the Air Transportation Safety and System Stabilization Act, enacted September 22, 2001; it initially operated from 2001 to 2004.

facts.label: Administration
facts.value: The Fund is administered by the U.S. Department of Justice under a Special Master appointed by the Attorney General.

facts.label: Eligibility scope
facts.value: The reopened VCF can compensate people with qualifying 9/11-related physical health conditions who can document presence at a covered site or exposure zone, as well as authorized representatives filing for deceased victims. Covered locations include the New York City exposure zone, the Pentagon site, and the Shanksville, Pennsylvania site during defined post-attack periods.

facts.label: Reauthorization and filing deadline
facts.value: The 2010 Zadroga Act reactivated the program, and the Never Forget the Heroes Act, enacted July 29, 2019, extended the deadline for claims and amendments to October 1, 2090 and provided funding for eligible claims.

facts.label: Legal framework
facts.value: The original program was designed as a no-fault alternative to certain civil litigation for physical injury and death caused by the September 11 attacks; awards take account of specified collateral-source payments under the governing law.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected timeline follows 25th-anniversary remembrance, advocacy, and related 9/11-records developments, not the full history of VCF claims processing, awards, eligibility decisions, or World Trade Center Health Program operations.
